prompt: What reaction does citrate synthase catalyze?

choices.text: The aldol-like addition of acetyl CoA to oxaloacetate to give citrate
The hydrolysis of citrate to acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate
choices.why: Citrate synthase builds citrate from acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate.

choices.text: The decarboxylation of oxaloacetate to give acetyl CoA
choices.why: No decarboxylation is involved; the reaction is an aldol-like addition.

choices.text: The transfer of a phosphate group from ATP to oxaloacetate
choices.why: That kind of reaction is catalyzed by kinases; citrate synthase forms a C–C bond in an aldol-like addition.

explanation: Citrate synthase catalyzes the aldol-like addition of acetyl CoA to oxaloacetate to give citrate (and HSCoA). This is the first step in the citric acid cycle.

prompt: What role does the citrate synthase reaction play in metabolism?

choices.text: It is the first step of the citric acid cycle, which metabolizes acetyl groups
It is the last step of the citric acid cycle, releasing acetyl CoA
choices.why: It is the first step, and it consumes acetyl CoA rather than releasing it.

choices.text: It is the first step of protein synthesis from amino acids
choices.why: Citrate synthase acts on acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate, not on amino acids.

choices.text: It converts CO2 and H2O into acetyl groups for storage
choices.why: The citric acid cycle runs the other way: acetyl groups are metabolized to CO2 and H2O.

explanation: The addition of acetyl CoA to oxaloacetate is the first step in the citric acid cycle, in which acetyl groups produced by degradation of food molecules are metabolized to yield CO2 and H2O.

prompt: How many amino acids make up the globular protein chain of citrate synthase?
explanation: Citrate synthase is a globular protein of 433 amino acids with a deep cleft lined by functional groups that bind the substrate, oxaloacetate.

prompt: Citrate synthase is dimeric: it consists of two identical chains of 433 amino acids each. How many amino acid residues does the dimer contain in total?
explanation: 2 × 433 = 866. The ribbon model in Figure 26.11.1 shows that the enzyme consists of two identical chains held together by hydrogen bonds and other intermolecular attractions.

prompt: What happens when citrate synthase binds oxaloacetate?

choices.text: The original cleft closes and another opens nearby to bind acetyl CoA
The enzyme releases acetyl CoA from a second, nearby cleft
choices.why: Acetyl CoA binds after oxaloacetate, in a newly opened cleft.

choices.text: The enzyme is denatured, exposing its hydrophobic interior
choices.why: Binding changes the shape of the clefts; it doesn't unfold the protein.

choices.text: Both clefts open wide so that the product citrate can enter
choices.why: Citrate is the product; binding oxaloacetate closes the first cleft and opens a second one for acetyl CoA.

explanation: Citrate synthase has a deep cleft that binds oxaloacetate. On binding oxaloacetate, the cleft closes and another opens nearby to bind acetyl CoA. This second cleft is lined by functional groups including a histidine at position 274 and an aspartic acid at position 375, which hold the two reactants close together in a suitable orientation.

prompt: In the first step of the citrate synthase mechanism, how is the enol of acetyl CoA formed?

choices.text: An aspartate side-chain carboxyl abstracts an acidic α proton while a histidine imidazole donates H+ to the carbonyl oxygen
A histidine imidazole abstracts the α proton while an aspartate donates H+ to the carbonyl oxygen
choices.why: The roles are reversed: the aspartate carboxylate is the base and the histidine is the acid.

choices.text: Water adds to the thioester carbonyl group
choices.why: Water hydrolyzes the thioester only at the end, in citryl CoA.

choices.text: Oxaloacetate abstracts the α proton directly
choices.why: Oxaloacetate is the electrophile that the enol adds to; enzyme side chains do the proton transfers.

explanation: The side-chain carboxyl of an aspartate residue acts as a base to abstract an acidic α proton from acetyl CoA, while at the same time the imidazole ring of a histidine donates H+ to the carbonyl oxygen. The result is the enol of acetyl CoA.

prompt: After the enol of acetyl CoA forms, what does it do in the citrate synthase mechanism?

choices.text: It performs a nucleophilic addition to the ketone carbonyl group of oxaloacetate
It is hydrolyzed by water to release coenzyme A
choices.why: Hydrolysis of the thioester comes last, after citryl CoA forms.

choices.text: It adds to the carboxylate group of oxaloacetate in a nucleophilic acyl substitution
choices.why: The enol adds to the ketone carbonyl group, in an aldol-like addition.

choices.text: It loses CO2 to give an acetyl radical
choices.why: No decarboxylation occurs; the enol acts as a nucleophile.

explanation: The enol performs a nucleophilic addition to the ketone carbonyl of oxaloacetate. The first histidine removes the –OH hydrogen from the enol, while a second histidine donates a proton to the oxaloacetate carbonyl, giving (S)-citryl CoA.

prompt: How many different histidine residues act as acid–base catalysts in the book's mechanism for citrate synthase?
explanation: One histidine donates H+ to the acetyl CoA carbonyl to form the enol and then removes the –OH hydrogen from the enol as it adds. A second histidine donates a proton to the oxaloacetate carbonyl group, giving citryl CoA.

prompt: How is citrate released at the end of the citrate synthase reaction?

choices.text: Water hydrolyzes the thiol ester of citryl CoA, releasing citrate and CoA
An aspartate removes coenzyme A from citryl CoA by an S_N2 reaction
choices.why: The final step is hydrolysis of the thioester by water.

choices.text: Citryl CoA loses CO2 from a carboxylate group to give citrate
choices.why: No decarboxylation occurs; water cleaves the thioester.

choices.text: A histidine reduces the thiol ester of citryl CoA to an alcohol
choices.why: The thioester is hydrolyzed, not reduced, giving the carboxylate of citrate.

explanation: In the last step, water hydrolyzes the thiol ester group in citryl CoA in a nucleophilic acyl substitution reaction, releasing citrate and coenzyme A as the final products.

prompt: According to Table 26.11.1, which coenzyme is matched with its function?

choices.text: Biotin: carboxylation
Thiamin diphosphate: methyl transfer
choices.why: Thiamin diphosphate is listed for decarboxylation; S-adenosylmethionine handles methyl transfer.

choices.text: Tetrahydrofolate: acyl transfer
choices.why: Tetrahydrofolate transfers C1 units; lipoic acid is listed for acyl transfer.

choices.text: Pyridoxal phosphate: decarboxylation
choices.why: Pyridoxal phosphate is listed for amino acid metabolism; thiamin diphosphate is the one for decarboxylation.

explanation: Table 26.11.1 lists tetrahydrofolate (transfer of C1 units), S-adenosylmethionine (methyl transfer), lipoic acid (acyl transfer), pyridoxal phosphate (amino acid metabolism), thiamin diphosphate (decarboxylation), and biotin (carboxylation).
